name: Reliever and preventer inhalers explained
headline: Reliever and preventer inhalers: what is the difference?
summary: A reliever inhaler eases symptoms when they happen; a preventer is used daily to calm airway inflammation. They do different jobs.
keyPoints: The NHS describes a reliever (such as blue salbutamol) as relieving symptoms when they occur and a preventer (a steroid such as beclometasone) as used every day to reduce airway inflammation.
Asthma + Lung UK says asthma guidelines do not recommend a blue reliever on its own, and suggests asking about a preventer or an AIR inhaler.
The NHS says to rinse the mouth or brush the teeth after a steroid inhaler to help prevent infections and a sore mouth; a spacer can help too.
Needing a reliever more often than usual can be a sign that asthma is not well controlled, according to the NHS and Asthma + Lung UK, and a GP or asthma nurse can review treatment.
In an asthma attack the NHS and Asthma + Lung UK say to call 999 if the reliever is not helping; NHS 111 and the GP cover non-urgent questions.

body.heading: What is the difference between a reliever and a preventer inhaler?
body.body: The NHS says the main treatment for asthma is medicine breathed in through an inhaler, and that for most people these medicines work well to reduce or prevent symptoms. A reliever inhaler is used when symptoms appear, and it quickly relaxes the airways so breathing becomes easier. A preventer inhaler is used every day, even when a person feels well, to help stop symptoms starting by reducing swelling and inflammation in the airways. The two do different jobs, and the NHS says a reliever is not meant to be given on its own when a preventer has also been prescribed.

body.heading: How does each type work?
body.body: A reliever opens the airways but does not treat the swelling underneath, because relievers contain no steroid. Salbutamol, the usual blue reliever, is a bronchodilator, meaning a medicine that widens the airways. A preventer such as beclometasone is an inhaled steroid, and the NHS says it needs to be used every day for it to work, even when there are no symptoms. Because a preventer works by calming inflammation, it does not help during an attack. In COPD, the NHS says short-acting bronchodilator inhalers are usually the first treatment, and a steroid inhaler may be added later for people who stay breathless or have frequent flare-ups.

body.heading: How are they used in general?
body.body: A reliever is used when symptoms occur, while a preventer is part of a daily routine. Asthma + Lung UK says current asthma guidelines do not recommend giving anyone with asthma only a blue reliever, and it suggests people ask a GP or asthma nurse about a preventer or an anti-inflammatory reliever, known as AIR. The exact medicine, device and plan are set by the prescriber, and the NHS says a person with asthma should have a written asthma action plan. Stopping or changing a preventer without advice is not recommended, so questions about this go to a GP, asthma nurse or pharmacist.

body.heading: What does a spacer do, and why check technique?
body.body: A spacer is a plastic chamber or tube that fits onto a pressurised metered-dose inhaler, the kind that sprays out a puff of medicine. The NHS says a spacer helps more of the medicine reach the lungs and makes the inhaler easier to use. Dry powder inhalers do not need one. The NHS says children and young people should always use their inhaler with a spacer. Asthma + Lung UK says a GP, nurse or pharmacist should show a person how to use their inhaler and spacer, and technique can also be checked at the annual asthma review. It also says a whistling sound from the spacer means the person is breathing in too fast.

body.heading: Should the mouth be rinsed after a steroid inhaler?
body.body: Yes, the NHS says to rinse the mouth or brush the teeth after using a steroid inhaler, to help prevent mouth infections and a sore mouth. Asthma + Lung UK gives similar advice, saying to rinse the mouth with water and spit it out if the inhaler contains steroid. The NHS adds that using a spacer with a beclometasone inhaler can also help prevent side effects in the mouth. A reliever such as salbutamol is not a steroid, and the rinsing advice in these sources is for steroid inhalers.

body.heading: What are the side effects?
body.body: The NHS says salbutamol has few side effects when used properly, and the common ones are shakiness, a faster heartbeat and headaches. It adds that these often ease or go away after the medicine has been used for a few days or weeks. Rarely, salbutamol can cause muscle pain, weakness or cramps, or an irregular heartbeat, which can be a sign of low potassium, and some people find the airways tighten after a dose. For beclometasone, the NHS lists oral thrush, a sore or dry throat and a hoarse voice as the most frequent effects. If thrush develops, the NHS says a pharmacist can suggest an antifungal mouth gel, and the inhaler is still used while the gel is used. A pharmacist or GP can advise on non-urgent side effects. The NHS says to call 999 for a serious allergic reaction, such as swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, or for new or worsening breathlessness or chest pain after salbutamol. If too much salbutamol has been used and the heartbeat is fast or noticeable, the NHS says to contact NHS 111.

body.heading: What can needing a reliever more often mean?
body.body: The NHS says needing salbutamol more often than usual may mean the condition is getting worse and that different treatment is needed. Asthma + Lung UK says that regularly needing a reliever inhaler is a sign that asthma is not well controlled, and it advises seeing the GP or asthma nurse. The NHS likewise advises speaking to a GP or asthma nurse if symptoms continue while using a preventer. This is usually a reason for a routine asthma review rather than an emergency, although a sudden worsening is different, as the next section sets out.

body.heading: When is it urgent?
body.body: The NHS and Asthma + Lung UK say that during an asthma attack a person uses their reliever inhaler as set out in their plan and calls 999 for an ambulance if the reliever is not helping. They say to call 999 as well if symptoms get worse at any point, or if there is worry at any time, or if there is no reliever inhaler and breathing is a struggle. Asthma + Lung UK says a person who feels able to get to hospital should still call 999, so treatment can begin on the way. After an attack, it says to ask for an urgent same-day appointment with the GP or nurse if the person managed it alone. For urgent advice that is not an emergency, NHS 111 is the route, and a GP appointment suits routine questions and the yearly asthma review.
